[BURSEVI:v6p98/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshāf laments that people have abandoned many religious practices as if they were abrogated, including seeking permission.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | One should say salām while seeking entry, ask three times, enter and greet again if permitted, and otherwise return.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Permission and greeting are better than entering suddenly, even into one’s mother’s home, since she might be unclothed.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | The rule guides Muslims away from the pre-Islamic habit of greeting a strange household with “good morning” or “good evening” on entry.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الكاشفي | reports | Kāshifī advises announcing one’s arrival at home by speaking, calling out, or clearing the throat so residents can cover themselves and prepare.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | “So that you may remember” depends on an omitted clause: the command was given so people would remember, take heed, and act accordingly.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Salām is a Muslim sunnah and the greeting of Paradise; it produces affection and removes resentment and rancor.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | A report says Adam sneezed, praised God, received God’s blessing, then greeted the assembled angels; God identified this as his greeting and his descendants’ greeting.
[BURSEVI:v6p98/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | A report lists six Muslim duties: greet on meeting, answer an invitation, counsel in absence, bless after a sneeze, visit the sick, and attend the funeral.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p133#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some understand your homes as homes where you reside, not homes you own; tenants and borrowers also need permission.

[ALUSI-FULL:v18p133/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | After prohibitions against zina and accusing chaste women, the passage addresses conduct that could lead to either and teaches manners conducive to happiness. | mentions 24:2, 24:4
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p133/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · امرأة من الأنصار | reports | An unnamed Ansari woman asked what to do when visitors entered during a private state that even children or parents should not see; the verse was revealed.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p133/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The possessive connection to your homes may express ownership; describing other homes reflects customary residence, though tenants and borrowers also need permission.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p134/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation derives istinas from intimacy, the opposite of alienation: it means permission, figuratively describing relief when uncertainty is resolved.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p134/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · النووي | prefers | Al-Nawawi prefers greeting before asking permission, citing reports that greetings precede speech and an un-greeted visitor is not admitted.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p134/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · جابر بن عبد الله | reports | Jabir reports the Prophet saying that greeting comes before speech.

[ALUSI-FULL:v18p134/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض الناس | reports | Supporters link the people-in-the-house reading to the next verse's case of finding no one there, but the author says this does not overcome the objections. | mentions 24:28

[ALUSI-FULL:v18p134/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A further explanation is that visitors notify the household through tasbih or a similar signal; the reports do not rule out earlier interpretations.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p134/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The people addressed by the greeting are the residents of the homes.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p134/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | The apparent order of the verse, as some read it, places asking permission before greeting.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Kashshaf says permission protects private conditions people ordinarily conceal from outsiders, not only against seeing nakedness; al-Alusi accepts it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Some grammarians supply an omitted clause: you were guided to this so that you may remember, take heed, and act accordingly.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The hadith that permission is due to looking states the common reason, not an exclusive one; inna-ma can emphasize without restricting the rule.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Permission and greeting are distinct, though some reports treat permission as part of greeting; without greeting it is as nothing.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبراهيم | reports | Ibrahim reports that Abd Allah's codex orders greeting the household and then asking permission.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | One explanation takes that to refer to entering by the permission and greeting understood from the wording.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Another explanation takes that to refer directly to the two acts of seeking permission and greeting.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The prescribed practice is better than sudden entry or pre-Islamic greetings; people sometimes entered and surprised a man with his wife under one blanket.

 entry to the Prophet's home by greeting and then asking whether he could enter.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أم إياس | reports | Umm Iyas recounts that Aisha initially refused entry to women until one greeted and asked permission, then invoked this verse.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The rule applies to women too; the masculine wording is inclusive, since householders may conceal private states from women as from men.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Sound reports say permission was instituted because of looking, so one should not peer into a house before asking.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو أمامة | reports | A report from the Prophet says a believer should not enter without permission and greeting; looking into a house counts as entry.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عبد الله بن بشر | reports | Abd Allah b. Bishr reports that the Prophet stood beside a doorway rather than facing it and greeted occupants, since doors then had no curtains.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The general address includes blind visitors, who may overhear private speech householders do not want them to hear.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الماوردي | reports | Al-Mawardi says greet first if the visitor has seen occupants; otherwise ask permission first.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Permission is most plainly requested by saying May I enter?; broader signals may qualify if they convey a request and alert the household.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عطاء | reports | According to a report from Ata, asking permission is obligatory for every adult; the verse's apparent wording allows one woman to provide it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قتادة | reports | Qatada describes three requests: the first alerts the household, the second lets them prepare, and the third leaves them free to admit or refuse.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | A marfu report through Abu Sa'id says that if permission is not granted after three requests, the visitor should leave.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | reports | Abu Hayyan says not to exceed three requests unless it is established that the household did not hear them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عطاء بن يسار | reports | A man asked whether he had to ask permission before entering on his mother each time; the Prophet asked whether he wished to see her naked, then told him to ask.
[ALUSI-FULL:v18p135/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud says people must ask permission before entering on their mothers and sisters.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · امرأة من الأنصار | reports | An unnamed woman from the Anṣār complained that a household member sometimes entered while she was in a state in which she did not want to be seen; the verse was revealed in response.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Where one has a right to enter but another person occupies the room, making oneself known is required; asking permission specifically is sunnah or etiquette rather than obligatory.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A judge who must enter a criminal's or suspect's home need not seek permission, but should still announce himself to avoid violating the occupant's honor.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Homes must be protected from intrusion and indecency, and their residents' security and peace respected by entering with proper etiquette through announcement and greeting.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · رسول الله | reports | A visitor who asked to enter using the blunt phrase “shall I penetrate?” was taught to say “peace be upon you; may I enter?”; only after repeating the proper formula was he admitted.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · رسول الله | reports | In the same report, the Prophet says that although God granted him much good, some knowledge is known only to God, and recites Luqmān 31:34. | mentions 31:34
[ELMALILI:24:27/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Pre-Islamic visitors disregarded the sanctity of the home and used greetings limited to morning or evening well-wishing; such greetings are not inherently bad, but reflect a horizon confined to worldly social wishes.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God teaches salām as a concise greeting promising unlimited well-being, broad enough to be the highest shared social ideal; relying only on other greetings instead is disliked as a remnant of jāhiliyya.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because salām is taught as the prescribed greeting, withholding it and relying on other greetings alone is makrūh.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · رسول الله | reports | Permission is sought three times: the first gives the household notice, the second allows them to prepare, and the third brings permission or refusal; after no answer at the third request, the visitor should leave.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The three requests should be spaced rather than made one after another, and the visitor should leave if no answer comes to the third.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Buyūt includes other people's houses or rooms; one must not enter them before making oneself known and greeting their occupants.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Loudly pounding on the door or shouting at the residents is forbidden because it disturbs and frightens them; al-Ḥujurāt 49:4 is sufficient prohibition in this matter. | mentions 49:4
[ELMALILI:24:27/r21] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The Prophet used to stand to the right or left of the door rather than directly facing it while seeking permission.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r22] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ebû Sa‘îd Hudrî | reports | When Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī sought permission while facing the door, the Prophet told him not to do so.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r23] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The practice protects visitors from suspicion, strengthens public security and order, and increases chastity and purity.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r24] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Tadhakkur means to remember, understand, and not forget.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r25] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · رسول الله | reports | When a man asked whether he must seek permission before entering his mother's room, the Prophet said yes; when he protested that he alone served her, the Prophet asked whether he wished to see her naked, and told him to ask permission.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Entering another person's property without permission is a usurpatory transgression, legally and judicially forbidden; even in one's own home, entering another person's room unannounced and without greeting is religiously and ethically prohibited.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · istînâsı istîzân diye tefsir edenler | reports | Some interpreters understand istīnās to mean seeking permission.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · istînâsı istikşâf-ı hâl ile isti‘lâm diye tefsir edenler | reports | Others understand istīnās as checking beforehand whether circumstances permit entry or finding out whether anyone is present.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | The apparent meaning is the opposite of startling the occupants: show sociable, humane consideration suited to the circumstances instead of barging in like a wild animal.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ebû Eyyub | reports | When asked what istīnās means, the Prophet reportedly said to notify the household by coughing, saying tasbīḥ, or saying takbīr.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Taslim means saying al-salāmu ʿalaykum; istīnās is broader than formal permission, encompassing gentle notification and announcement, which explains the verse's wording.
[ELMALILI:24:27/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Permission is always required to enter a home where one has no ownership or right of entry; otherwise entry is an assault and the householder may defend himself.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p196/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | These rules advance the surah’s broader aim of regulating social and family dealings among neighbors, introducing visitation and permission etiquette so people follow a clear common procedure.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p196/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Permission was known in pre-Islamic times and early Islam but varied by the visitor’s status and could be skipped or abbreviated; these verses standardize it as religious etiquette.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p196/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A visitor may be intent on satisfying an immediate need, while an unannounced or hurried entry can embarrass or burden the host; the prescribed etiquette guards against this.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p196/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Homes shelter people from heat, cold, rain, and dust, and protect private matters from unwanted exposure; a resident needs time to prepare or conceal them before admitting a visitor or speaking outside.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p196/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · مالك | reports | Mālik, as transmitted by Ibn Wahb, takes tastaʾnisū as seeking permission, glossing it as seeking welcome or familiarity with the homeowner.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p196/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn Ashur endorses Mālik’s interpretation as decisive: the expression is a subtle metonymy for seeking permission, in a manner that will not make the householder uneasy.

[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | These rulings continue the fitting sequence of legal instructions in the passage.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r10] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The preceding verse covers entry when the person authorized to admit is present and does not refuse; verse 28 covers houses with no such person present.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Uns means affinity and a settled heart; istiʾnās is seeking that familiarity by signaling—such as remembering God or clearing one's throat—so a householder knows someone wants to enter.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The signal lets residents prepare before being seen in a private state; the rule protects their privacy and the dignity of faith.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Signaling before entry and then greeting the residents helps conceal private matters and reassures them that the visitor poses no threat.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Maintaining this practice strengthens brotherhood, affection, and mutual cooperation in showing what is good and covering what is shameful, foundations of social happiness.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The verse's reminder points to the duties of preserving brotherhood and united hearts through which social well-being is sustained.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | An alternative supplies an omitted phrase: the rule was given so people would recall God's admonitions and act accordingly; the author allows this reading.
[TABATABAI:24:27-29/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | rejects | A proposed transposition puts greeting before signaling; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects it.
[TABATABAI:24:27-34/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · أبو أيوب الأنصاري | reports | Asked what istiʾnās means, the Prophet says to announce oneself to the household with tasbīḥ, taḥmīd, takbīr, or throat-clearing; al-Durr al-manthūr also transmits this report.
[TABATABAI:24:27-34/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · سهل بن سعد | reports | When a man peered into one of the Prophet's chambers, the Prophet threatened to pierce his eye with a comb and explained that permission is required to prevent looking; al-Durr al-manthūr also transmits it.
[TABATABAI:24:27-34/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · رسول الله | reports | A man asks whether he must seek permission to enter upon his mother each time; the Prophet asks whether he would want to see her naked, and he agrees permission is necessary.

[TABATABAI:24:27-34/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · عبادة بن الصامت | reports | A report transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh says that whoever lets his eye enter before asking permission and greeting has disobeyed God and has no permission.

[ASAD-NOTES:24:27#n33/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The rule establishes each person's home and private life as inviolable, with wider socio-political implications.

[BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p218/r3] BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 · author | holds | The Arabic sense of īnās is not a bare formal permission, and ānasa is unsuitable for seeing an enemy or fire or hearing thunder or a beast's roar.
